title: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
summary: Why LLMs read subwords, how BPE learns a merge list by counting adjacent pairs, how encoding replays merges by rank, how GPT-2's byte-level BPE handles any text, and the failure modes that follow.
outcomes: Explain why word-level and character-level tokenization both fail and how subwords fix it
Run BPE training by hand: count weighted adjacent pairs, merge the top pair, repeat
Encode an unseen word by applying merges in rank order, and explain why order matters
Explain byte-level BPE in GPT-2: 256 byte base tokens, regex pre-tokenization, leading spaces
Predict tokenizer failure modes for numbers, non-English text and under-trained tokens

lessons.title: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters

blocks.md: A language model cannot read text directly. It reads a list of integers, one per **token**, where each integer indexes a row of an **embedding table**: a learned matrix with one vector per entry of the **vocabulary**. If the vocabulary has $V$ entries and each vector has $d$ numbers, the table holds $V \times d$ parameters. A **tokenizer** is the fixed procedure that turns a string into those integers and back.

So the first design question is: what should one token be? There are two obvious answers, and both break.

- **One token per word.** Short sequences, but the vocabulary must list every word. A word not in the list (a new name, a typo, a rare inflection) becomes a single catch-all `<unk>` (unknown) token and its meaning is lost.
- **One token per character.** A tiny vocabulary and nothing is ever unknown, but sequences get several times longer, and every extra position costs compute and uses up the model's fixed context window.

blocks.title: How many units does one sentence cost?

scenes.caption: The sentence "Tokenization is unbelievably useful." is 36 characters and 36 bytes (it is plain ASCII). A character model must process 36 positions.
Splitting on spaces gives just 4 words, but only if every word, including "unbelievably" and "useful." with its period, is in the vocabulary.
GPT-2's byte-level BPE tokenizer uses 6 tokens: Token, ization, " is", " unbelievably", " useful", ".". Close to word length, yet it can spell any string.

blocks.md: **Subword** tokenization sits between the two. Frequent words get their own token, and rare words are spelled out of smaller, reusable pieces. Sennrich, Haddow and Birch brought this to neural machine translation in 2016 using BPE, arguing that a fixed vocabulary of variable-length character sequences can represent an *open* vocabulary: any word, including ones never seen in training.

blocks.title: One rare word at three granularities

scenes.caption: Character level: 12 tokens for one word. Nothing is unknown, but each token carries little meaning on its own.
GPT-2's tokenizer (vocabulary 50,257) writes "unbelievably" with no leading space as 4 pieces. Note "un" and "ably": pieces that recur across many words.

GPT-4's cl100k_base tokenizer (vocabulary about 100k) needs only 3 pieces. A bigger vocabulary can store longer pieces, so sequences are usually shorter, though not always: mid-sentence " unbelievably" is 1 GPT-2 token but 2 in cl100k_base.

blocks.md: The price of a bigger vocabulary is a bigger embedding table. GPT-2's smallest model has $d = 768$ and $V = 50{,}257$, so its token embedding alone is $50{,}257 \times 768 = 38{,}597{,}376$ parameters, about a third of the 117M parameters the GPT-2 paper reports for that model. Vocabulary size is therefore a real tradeoff, not a free knob.

A subword tokenizer gives you short sequences for common text **and** no unknown words, because anything rare can always fall back to smaller pieces. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is the most widely used way to choose those pieces.

A token is not a word. In GPT-2, " hello" (with its leading space) and "hello" are two different tokens with different ids, and many common words are split. Counting words is a poor estimate of token count.

blocks.question: A word-level model with a 50,000-word vocabulary meets the made-up product name "Zorblax" at inference. What happens?
options: It maps to the single unknown token, so the model cannot tell it apart from any other unknown word
It is split into characters automatically
It is added to the vocabulary on the fly
The model raises an error and stops
blocks.explain: A word-level vocabulary is fixed after training. Any word outside it becomes the shared `<unk>` id, losing its identity. Falling back to smaller pieces is exactly what a subword tokenizer adds; a pure word-level one has no such fallback.

blocks.question: You double a model's vocabulary size, keeping everything else fixed. Which pair of effects should you expect?
options: Longer sequences and a smaller embedding table
No change in sequence length, only more parameters
Shorter token sequences for the same text, and a larger embedding table
Shorter sequences and fewer parameters
blocks.explain: More vocabulary entries let the tokenizer keep longer pieces, so the same text needs fewer tokens. But each new entry is another row of $d$ numbers in the embedding table (and in the output layer that predicts the next token).

lessons.title: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat

blocks.md: BPE began in 1994 as a compression trick by Gage: repeatedly replace the most frequent pair of adjacent bytes with a new, unused byte. Sennrich et al. adapted it to text: start from characters and repeatedly **merge** the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols into a new symbol. Each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary, so the final vocabulary size is the starting alphabet plus the number of merges, and the number of merges is the only hyperparameter.

We will run the exact toy corpus from Sennrich et al.'s paper. The training text has been reduced to a word list with counts: *low* 5 times, *lower* 2, *newest* 6, *widest* 3. Each word is written as characters followed by an end-of-word marker (the paper writes `</w>`; we show `_`). The marker lets the model tell a suffix such as "est at the end of a word" from the same letters mid-word.

blocks.tex: \text{count}(a,b) = \sum_{w} \text{freq}(w) \cdot \#\{\text{positions where } a \text{ is immediately followed by } b \text{ in } w\}
blocks.caption: Pairs are counted inside words only (Sennrich et al. skip pairs that cross word boundaries), weighted by how often each word occurs.

blocks.title: Pair counts before and after the first merges

scenes.caption: Initial counts. Three pairs tie at 9: (e, s), (s, t), (t, _), each from newest (6) plus widest (3). (w, e) has 8: 6 from newest and 2 from lower.
After merging (e, s): that pair is gone, and (s, t) also drops to 0 because every s is now inside es. (w, e) falls from 8 to 2, since newest now reads w then es. A new pair (es, t) has 9.
After merging (es, t) into est, (t, _) drops to 0 as well. The top pair is now the new (est, _) with 9. Only pairs touching a merged symbol changed; the rest kept their counts.

blocks.title: The corpus as merges are applied

scenes.caption: Start: every word is split into characters plus an end-of-word marker (shown as _). Counts on the left are word frequencies in the training text. Writing the corpus takes 95 symbols.
Merge 1: (e, s) occurs 9 times (6 in newest, 3 in widest), tied with (s, t) and (t, _). The tie goes to the pair seen first. Every e s becomes one symbol es. 86 symbols.
Merge 2: counts are recomputed. The new pair (es, t) now has 9 occurrences and wins. 77 symbols.
Merge 3: (est, _) with 9. The token est_ means "est at the end of a word", which is different from est in the middle of one. 68 symbols.
Merge 4: (l, o), 7 occurrences (5 in low, 2 in lower), tied with (o, w). 61 symbols.
Merge 5: (lo, w), 7. The whole word low is now a single symbol in both low and lower. 54 symbols.
Merge 6: (n, e), 6, tied with (e, w) and (w, est_). 48 symbols.
Merge 7: (ne, w), 6. Merge 8 would create newest_ (6 times), then low_ (5), then wi (3). After 10 merges the corpus takes 28 symbols.

blocks.prompt: The starting alphabet here is 11 symbols (l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d and _). After 10 merges, how big is the vocabulary, and how many symbols does it take to write the whole weighted corpus?
blocks.reveal: The vocabulary is $11 + 10 = 21$ symbols, because each merge adds exactly one. The corpus shrinks from **95** symbols to **28**: low is one token (low_), newest is one token (newest_), lower is low e r _ and widest is wi d est_. That shrinking is the compression BPE inherited from Gage's algorithm.

blocks.caption: Close to Algorithm 1 in Sennrich et al. (2016). The output, in order: (e,s) (es,t) (est,</w>) (l,o) (lo,w) (n,e) (ne,w) (new,est</w>) (low,</w>) (w,i).

blocks.md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

Ties are common on small data. This code picks the pair it encountered first, so a different tie-break or a different word order can produce a different merge list. Real trainers fix a deterministic rule; production implementations also update pair counts incrementally instead of recounting everything, as Sennrich et al. note.

blocks.question: Starting from the initial corpus, suppose newest appeared 9 times instead of 6 (everything else unchanged). Which pair would be merged first?
options: (e, s), still tied with (s, t) and (t, _) at 12
(l, o), because low is the most frequent word
(w, e), which rises to 11
(n, e), because newest is now the most frequent word
blocks.explain: Each of (e, s), (s, t), (t, _) becomes $9 + 3 = 12$, and (w, e) becomes $9 + 2 = 11$. The top count is a three-way tie at 12, and the first-seen rule picks (e, s). Word frequency alone does not decide: (l, o) gets 7 and (n, e) gets 9.

blocks.question: Why does the training corpus become a list of (word, count) pairs before BPE starts?
options: Because BPE only works on English
Because the end-of-word marker requires it
Because it removes rare words
Because pairs are never counted across word boundaries, so identical words can be processed once and weighted by their count
blocks.explain: Sennrich et al. do not count pairs that cross word boundaries. Then every occurrence of the same word behaves identically, so the algorithm can run on the word dictionary with each word weighted by its frequency, which is far faster than scanning the raw text each step.

lessons.title: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order

blocks.md:
Training gave us an ordered merge list. Here are the 10 merges from the toy corpus with their **rank** (1 = learned first):

1. e s
2. es t
3. est _
4. l o
5. lo w
6. n e
7. ne w
8. new est_
9. low _
10. w i

To encode a word, split it into characters plus `_`, then repeat one step: among all adjacent pairs currently in the word, find the one with the **lowest rank** and merge every occurrence of it. Stop when no adjacent pair appears in the merge list. This is exactly what GPT-2's released `encoder.py` does: its `bpe` function picks the bigram with the minimum rank on each pass.

blocks.title: Encoding lowest, a word never seen in training
blocks.code:
def encode_word(word, ranks):
    parts = list(word) + ["_"]
    while len(parts) > 1:
        pairs = [(parts[i], parts[i + 1])
                 for i in range(len(parts) - 1)]
        best = min(pairs,
                   key=lambda p: ranks.get(p, INF))
        if best not in ranks:
            break
        parts = merge(parts, best)
    return parts

scenes.caption: Split into characters plus the end marker. lowest did not occur in the training corpus.

vars.parts: l o w e s t _

scenes.caption: Candidate pairs: (l,o) rank 4, (o,w) unranked, (w,e) unranked, (e,s) rank 1, (s,t) unranked, (t,_) unranked. Lowest rank wins: (e,s).

vars.parts: l o w e s t _

scenes.caption: Merge it. Ranks, not counts in this word, decide the order: the tokenizer replays training's choices.
Next lowest rank present is (es, t), rank 2.
Then (est, _), rank 3, which builds the word-final suffix token.
Then (l, o) rank 4 and (lo, w) rank 5.
The only pair left, (low, est_), is not in the merge list, so the loop stops. An unseen word became 2 known tokens.

blocks.md: Notice what happened: the training text had *low* and *newest* but never *lowest*, yet the result is two meaningful pieces, a stem and a suffix. This is how a subword model handles words it has never seen. Decoding is the reverse and is trivial: concatenate the token strings and turn each `_` back into a word boundary, so `low` + `est_` gives back "lowest ".

blocks.prompt: The word lower *was* in the training corpus (2 times). With these 10 merges, how many tokens does it encode to?
blocks.reveal: **4 tokens: low, e, r, _.** Training never merged (e, r) or (r, _) because those pairs only occurred 2 times and lost to more frequent pairs within the 10-merge budget. Being in the training data does not guarantee a word becomes one token; only frequency does. (Sennrich et al.'s paper shows a different toy corpus where er_ is learned, so lower becomes low er_.)

scenes.caption: Final encodings with the 10 toy merges. Common pieces (low, new, est_) are reused across words.
Rare material falls back to single characters (e, r, _, s). That fallback is why nothing is ever unknown, as long as every character is in the alphabet.

blocks.md: Some vocabulary entries are only stepping stones. In the toy, ne exists only to build new, and es only to build est. Sennrich et al. give a real case: safeguar, whose every training occurrence was absorbed into safeguard, so it never appears as a final token. In GPT-2 style tokenizers every merge result, stepping stone or not, still gets its own vocabulary id.

Encoding is **not** "find the longest matching token from the left" and not "pick the segmentation with fewest tokens". BPE applies merges greedily in the order they were learned. A different procedure over the same vocabulary can give a different split, and the model was trained on BPE's split.

blocks.question: Encode newer with the 10 toy merges. What comes out?
options: new e r _
new er_
n e w e r _
ne w e r _
blocks.explain: Pairs present at the start: (n,e) rank 6, (e,w) and others unranked. Merge (n,e), then (ne,w) rank 7 gives new. Remaining pairs (new,e), (e,r), (r,_) are not in the list, so the result is new e r _. No er_ token was learned.

blocks.question: A teammate's encoder, given lowest, first merges (l, o) because l o is the leftmost pair present in the merge list. Is the final result different here, and what is the bug?
options: Different result; the merge list should be applied left to right
Same result here, but the rule is wrong: merges must be applied by lowest rank, and on other inputs left to right gives splits the model never saw
Same result, and the rule is fine since merges commute
Different result; BPE merges the most frequent pair in the current word
blocks.explain: For lowest both orders happen to end at low est_. But BPE's contract is rank order: the encoder must reproduce the segmentation used during training. Merges do not commute in general (merging one pair can destroy an overlapping one), so a left-to-right encoder can disagree with the model's training data on other inputs.

lessons.title: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything

blocks.md: Character-level BPE has a hole: a character missing from the training alphabet (an emoji, a rare script) still becomes unknown. Simply putting every Unicode character into the base vocabulary is too expensive. The GPT-2 paper notes this would mean a base vocabulary of over 130,000 before any merges, against the 32,000 to 64,000 token vocabularies typical for BPE.

GPT-2's fix is **byte-level BPE**. Text is first encoded as UTF-8, a variable-length encoding where ASCII characters take 1 byte and others take 2 to 4 (é is the two bytes 195 169; the Devanagari letter न is three bytes 224 164 168). BPE then starts from the 256 possible byte values instead of characters. Every string is a byte sequence, so **no input can be unknown**. GPT-2's vocabulary is 50,257: 256 byte tokens, 50,000 merges and one special `<|endoftext|>` token.

Run naively on bytes, BPE wastes slots. The GPT-2 authors saw it learn many variants like `dog.` `dog!` `dog?`. So before BPE, a **pre-tokenizer** splits text into chunks with a regular expression, and merges never cross chunk boundaries. GPT-2's pattern keeps letters, digits and punctuation in separate chunks, splits off common English contractions (`'s`, `'t`, `'ll`, ...), and attaches a single leading space to the following word.

blocks.title: Pre-tokenization, then BPE inside each chunk

scenes.caption: The regex splits "Hello world!! It's 2024." into 7 chunks (here _ marks a space, not lesson 2's end-of-word marker). The space sticks to the start of the next word; letters, digits and punctuation land in separate chunks, and 's is its own chunk.
GPT-2's merges happen to cover each chunk fully, so 7 chunks give 7 tokens. Real text is usually less tidy: longer or rarer chunks split into several tokens.
GPT-4's cl100k_base uses a different regex: numbers are cut into runs of at most 3 digits, and the space before them stands alone. Same text, 9 tokens.

blocks.title: The full encode path for naïve café

scenes.caption: Input: 10 characters, but ï and é are 2 bytes each in UTF-8, so 12 bytes.
The GPT-2 regex yields two chunks: "naïve" and " café" (with its leading space). Merges will stay inside each chunk.
Each chunk becomes bytes: 6 bytes and 6 bytes. Every one of the 256 byte values is already a token, so the worst case is one token per byte.
Merges are replayed by rank inside each chunk, exactly as in the previous lesson but over bytes.
Result with GPT-2: na | ïve | " café", ids 2616, 38776, 40304. Three tokens for 12 bytes.

blocks.prompt: In GPT-2, "unbelievably" with no leading space is 4 tokens (un, bel, iev, ably). How many tokens is " unbelievably" with a leading space, as it would appear mid-sentence?
blocks.reveal: **One token** (id 48943). Because the regex glues the space onto the word, the mid-sentence form " unbelievably" is a distinct, much more frequent string, and BPE learned it whole. The same word at the start of a text, or after a newline, is a different and often longer token sequence. Prompts that end in a trailing space can therefore look unusual to the model.

blocks.md: If you open GPT-2's vocabulary file you will see tokens like `Ġworld`. That `Ġ` is not a typo: `encoder.py` maps each of the 256 bytes to a printable Unicode character so that the BPE code never handles raw whitespace or control bytes, and the space byte (32) is shown as `Ġ` (U+0120). It is only a display convention for the vocabulary files; the token still means the bytes " world".

blocks.code:
import tiktoken

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("gpt2")
ids = enc.encode("naïve café")
print(ids)                     # [2616, 38776, 40304]
print([enc.decode_single_token_bytes(i) for i in ids])
# [b'na', b'\xc3\xafve', b' caf\xc3\xa9']
assert enc.decode(ids) == "naïve café"   # lossless round trip
print(enc.n_vocab)             # 50257
blocks.caption: OpenAI's tiktoken library ships the GPT-2, cl100k_base (GPT-4) and o200k_base (GPT-4o) encodings. Output shown is from running this code.

blocks.md: Byte-level BPE = UTF-8 bytes as the base alphabet (256 symbols, so nothing is ever unknown) + a regex pre-tokenizer that limits where merges can happen + an ordered merge list. Decoding concatenates bytes and is lossless.

blocks.question: Why can GPT-2's tokenizer encode an emoji it never saw during tokenizer training, without an unknown token?
options: It has a fallback table of every Unicode character
The regex deletes characters it does not recognise
It maps any unseen character to the nearest known one
The emoji is UTF-8 bytes, and all 256 byte values are base tokens, so it can always be written as bytes
blocks.explain: The base vocabulary is the 256 byte values. Any string, emoji included, is a sequence of UTF-8 bytes, so in the worst case each byte is its own token. Merges only make common byte sequences shorter.

blocks.question: The GPT-2 regex has no case-insensitive flag, and its source code carries a comment saying it should have had one. What does that cause for the text I'LL?
options: I'LL is one token
The contraction is not recognised: it splits as I | ' | LL
The regex lowercases it to i'll
It raises an error
blocks.explain: The contraction alternatives are lowercase ('ll, 're, ...), so 'LL does not match them. The apostrophe falls into the punctuation alternative and LL into the letters alternative, giving I, ', LL. The cl100k_base pattern wraps the contractions in a case-insensitive group.

lessons.title: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives

blocks.md: Tokenization is decided once, before the model trains, and every later behaviour inherits it. This lesson covers the main knobs and the problems they cause in real systems.

**Vocabulary size.** The larger $V$ is, the shorter sequences get, but the embedding table (and the output layer that scores every token) grows linearly in $V$. The plot below is just $V \times d$, the number of embedding parameters, for a width $d$ you can change.

blocks.title: Embedding parameters grow linearly with vocabulary size

scenes.caption: At GPT-2 small's width (768), its 50,257-token vocabulary costs 38.6M embedding parameters, about a third of the 117M model.
At width 4096, a 200k vocabulary would cost about 819M parameters for the embedding table alone. In a large model that is a small fraction; in a small one it dominates.

blocks.md: **Numbers.** BPE merges whatever digit strings were frequent, so the same number can split unpredictably. LLaMA's tokenizer avoids this by splitting every number into individual digits. OpenAI's cl100k_base regex instead cuts digit runs into chunks of at most 3, starting from the left.

scenes.caption: GPT-2 on "2024 + 1999 = 4023" (_ marks a space): 2024 splits 20|24, 1999 is one token, 4023 splits 40|23. Each number gets a different structure, which makes digit-wise arithmetic harder to learn.
cl100k_base: every number is chopped into 3 digits then the rest (202|4, 199|9, 402|3), so the structure is at least consistent. 10 tokens instead of 7.

blocks.md: **Languages.** A tokenizer trained mostly on English learns long merges for English and few for other scripts. Petrov et al. (2023) measured the same text translated into different languages and found token counts differing by up to 15 times. Since API pricing, latency and context limits are counted in tokens, this is a real cost difference between users.

blocks.title: Tokens for "Hello, how are you?" in three languages

scenes.caption: UTF-8 bytes: 19 for English, 50 for the Hindi "नमस्ते, आप कैसे हैं?" (each Devanagari character is 3 bytes) and 30 for the Russian "Привет, как дела?" (Cyrillic letters are 2 bytes). Byte-level BPE starts from these.
GPT-2 (50k, English-heavy training data): 6, 32 and 18 tokens. Hindi costs over 5x the English tokens for the same greeting.
GPT-4's cl100k_base: 6, 20 and 8 tokens.

GPT-4o's o200k_base: 6, 9 and 6 tokens. A bigger vocabulary with more non-English merges narrows the gap; it does not close it for every language. Single example: see Petrov et al. for systematic measurements.

blocks.md: **Glitch tokens.** The tokenizer and the model are often trained on different data. A string frequent in the tokenizer's data but almost absent from the model's training data gets its own token whose embedding is barely trained. The famous example is " SolidGoldMagikarp", a single GPT-2 token (id 43453). Land and Bartolo (2024) built methods to detect such under-trained tokens and found them across many models.

**Alternatives to plain BPE.**

- **WordPiece** (BERT) also merges bottom-up but scores a pair by $\text{count}(ab) / (\text{count}(a)\,\text{count}(b))$, preferring pairs that co-occur more than chance predicts.
- **Unigram LM** (Kudo, 2018) starts from a large candidate vocabulary, prunes the pieces that matter least to a probabilistic model, and can *sample* different segmentations during training. Bostrom and Durrett (2020) pretrained identical models with each and found Unigram matched or beat BPE on downstream tasks.
- **BPE-dropout** (Provilkov et al., 2020) keeps the BPE merge list but randomly drops merges while segmenting training data, exposing the model to multiple splits; plain BPE is used at inference.
- **SentencePiece** is a library that runs BPE or Unigram on raw text, treating the space as an ordinary symbol written `▁`, so it works for languages without spaces.

blocks.question: On the toy corpus from lesson 2, (e, s) occurs 9 times; e occurs 17 times and s 9 times. (i, d) occurs 3 times; i and d occur 3 times each. Which pair does the WordPiece score pick first, and which does BPE pick?
options: Both pick (e, s)
WordPiece picks (i, d) with score 1/3; BPE picks (e, s) with count 9
WordPiece picks (e, s) with score 9/153; BPE picks (i, d)
Both pick (i, d)
blocks.explain: WordPiece: $9/(17 \cdot 9) \approx 0.059$ for (e, s) versus $3/(3 \cdot 3) \approx 0.333$ for (i, d), the highest of any pair since i and d only ever appear together. BPE ignores the individual frequencies and takes the raw top count, (e, s) with 9.

blocks.question: Your model is weak at multi-digit addition, and you are designing the tokenizer for its successor. Which change most directly targets the problem?
options: Double the vocabulary so more numbers become single tokens
Remove the end-of-text token
Make numbers tokenize consistently, for example one token per digit as LLaMA does
Switch from UTF-8 to UTF-16 bytes
blocks.explain: The problem is that the same digits land in different token groupings depending on what BPE happened to merge. Splitting digits individually (LLaMA) or into fixed-size groups (cl100k) gives a consistent structure. A bigger vocabulary makes more numbers single opaque tokens, which hides their digits from the model.

blocks.md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.
